metadata.title: The Protective Factor of Resilience in the Face of Mathematical Anxiety

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study used a convenience sample of 1742 high school students from secondary schools in the province of Almeria (Spain) and collected self-report questionnaires plus end-of-year mathematics grades. The manuscript does not describe the use of any international large-scale assessment microdata, nor does it report any complex survey design features (stratification, clustering) or the application of sampling/survey weights. Because the analysis is based on a local school-based sample and employs SEM with bootstrapping rather than ILSA plausible-value achievement modeling, standard ILSA weight variables (e.g., student weights) are not applicable here. Consequently, the results should be interpreted as associations within this regional sample rather than population-representative estimates.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are questionnaire-based psychological constructs (academic resilience, mathematical anxiety, motivation, metacognitive strategies) and students’ end-of-year mathematics grades, not ILSA cognitive achievement scores generated via plausible values. Therefore, plausible values handling is not applicable because the study does not use PV-based achievement scales from PISA/TIMSS/other ILSA instruments. The manuscript also does not report any missing-data handling procedure (e.g., listwise deletion or imputation), so the missing-data strategy cannot be evaluated from the provided text.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were 1742 high school students (958 boys, 784 girls) aged 13–16 (mean 14.87, SD 1.17) from several secondary schools in the province of Almeria, Spain. The manuscript does not specify additional inclusion/exclusion criteria beyond school participation and informed consent, and it does not report any task-level or item-level filtering (e.g., questionnaire completeness thresholds) or missing-data exclusions. Questionnaires were administered at the beginning of mathematics class with an estimated completion time of 25 minutes.

main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using ILSA assessment context not specified in extraction (heuristic migration) the study leveraged Academic resilience, Mathematical anxiety, Self-determination index (SDI) to predict predicting SDI (β = 0, finding that This cross-sectional study analyzed 1742 students from secondary schools in Almeria (Spain) to examine how academic resilience and mathematical anxiety relate to motivation, metacognitive strategies, and end-of-year mathematics performance. The authors used SEM with maximum likelihood estimation and bootstrapping (5000 interactions) to test a hypothesized predictive model, reporting good model fit (χ2/df = 2.41, CFI = 0.96, IFI = 0.96, TLI = 0.96, RMSEA = 0.053, SRMR = 0.041). Key standardized paths showed resilience negatively associated with mathematical anxiety (β = −0.54, p < 0.001), resilience positively predicting SDI (β = 0.43, p < 0.001) and metacognitive strategies (β = 0.57, p < 0.001), and anxiety negatively predicting SDI (β = −0.47, p < 0.001) and metacognitive strategies (β = −0.31, p < 0.01). Motivation (SDI) predicted metacognitive strategies (β = 0.43, p < 0.001) and academic performance (β = 0.48, p < 0.001), and metacognitive strategies predicted performance (β = 0.55, p < 0.001). Limitations include the absence of any reported missing-data handling and the inability to infer causality due to the cross-sectional design. This indicates that these patterns have implications for educational policy and instructional practice, though cross-sectional ILSA designs cannot establish causality.

data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction is sparse with respect to ILSA/ML because the manuscript is not an empirical machine-learning study using ILSA microdata; it is a questionnaire-based SEM analysis on a regional convenience sample. As a result, there are no ILSA program/cycle/domain elements, no plausible-value handling, and no ML algorithms or predictive performance metrics (e.g., accuracy/AUC/RMSE) to extract. The main quantitative results are reported as SEM fit indices and standardized path coefficients rather than ML model evaluation.
